temperaments.name: Meantone
temperaments.description: Tempers out 81/80. Quarter-comma ~696.6¢. Four fifths = major third (5/4).

temperaments.name: Flattone
temperaments.description:
Flat meantone. 7/4 maps to diminished seventh. ~695¢ fifth. So if you ever want to hit a harmonic seventh here, just diminish your minor 7 by an edostep.

26edo is the quintessential flattone tuning, which can pretty much perfectly tune the 7th harmonic. No other reasonably sized edo comes even close to nailing 7/4. If you want meantone vibes but with more xenharmonic street cred, this is your guy. Though if you were looking for "normal music but with an in-tune 7/4" you're out of luck 'cus this guy's fifths are very out of tune.

temperaments.name: Deeptone
temperaments.description:
Very flat meantone. Near 1/2-comma meantone, between flattone and 7edo. 11 fifths ~= 5/4, so the optimal generator is around 689.7c.

We'tre basically hovering around 7edo at this point. 33edo and 40edo are the simplest edos that can construct this temperament, which isn't ideal. While flattone has terrible fifths, in exchange it at least gives you a great 7/4.

Deeptone on the other hand just has bad fifths. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

temperaments.name: Pythagorean
temperaments.description:
Pure 3/2 at 701.955¢. Near-just intonation of 3-limit. Basically all western music comes from this.

Be careful when exploring tunings outside of this range. You may encounter critics who insist your music sounds "bad" and "out of tune" and you should "get a job" and to "stop living in your moms basement memorizing made up names all day".

temperaments.name: Parapyth
temperaments.description:
Rank-3 (2.3.7.11.13). Near-pure, slightly sharp fifths with 7/11/13 mapping. Something like 46edo does this very well, with a ~2c sharp 3/2 in comparison to the 12edo 2c flat 3/2. Same tuning discrepency but in the other direction.

Technically parapyth is a rank-3 temperament, but the only alternative was to call this range "pepperoni" which I simply refuse to do.

temperaments.name: Superpyth
temperaments.description: Sharp fifths. Two fifths = 8/7. Opposite of meantone. 22 and 27edo are quintissential superpyth tunings. Sounds snazzy - classic xen sound.

temperaments.name: Ultrapyth
temperaments.description:
Very sharp fifths near 5edo. 5/4 mapped to +14 fifths.

The diatonic scale starts to collapse melodically here; composition may be tricky.

Some weird stuff can happen where the extremely small comma-step can give you a just 3/2 again, by correcting your very sharp superpyth fifth.

temperaments.name: Gravity
temperaments.description: The very bottom of the diatonic fifth, just barely flat of 7edo before it collapses into mavila. Fifths this flat are on the edge of no longer functioning as fifths, but the scale still reads as diatonic rather than antidiatonic.

temperaments.name: Mavila
temperaments.description:
Anti-diatonic. The bees knees. Very flat fifths, four fifths = 6/5 instead of 5/4.

In this range, major chords invert into minor chords and vice versa. Diminished chords become augmented chords. Timbre matters a lot here to compensate and navigate around the fact that your 3/2 is so flat.
Approximates some Gamelan tunings as well.

Note: sharp of 680¢, six flat fifths produce a more in-tune 4/3 than a single fourth.

temperaments.name: Trismegistus
temperaments.description:
The 7-limit extension of mabilic, where 5/2 splits into three generators. In the flatter, 7-limit region of mavila - you can find a nice 7/4, 8/7, 9/7, 14/9 etc here, as well as a near-just 5/4 major third.

Can simultaneously represent a magic temperament (3 is 15 generators away, so five near-major-thirds stack up) as well as slendric/tricot (8/7 at 5 generators).

25edo, 41edo, and 66edo are the sweet spots. Beyond the goated 2L 5s antidiatonic, its 9L 7s MOS is also pretty good; 3/2 shows up as the "augmented" flavor of the generator. Flatter than mavila, so the fifth has drifted even further from home.

temperaments.name: Amavil
temperaments.description:
A subset temperament of Mavila; using generator a flat ~35/24 (~670¢).

The flattest corner of the antidiatonic fifth before it stops feeling like a fifth at all. Any flatter and the 7L 2s equalizes into 9edo. Nudging the generator loses most of the 7-limit intervals in Trismegistus, but buys you in exchange especially weird 7/6 superparticular interval.

temperaments.name: Wilsec
temperaments.description:
2.3.7 subgroup. Divides the 12th harmonic into 8 equal parts. Therefor, 8 generators will give you a 3/2 here. Tempers out 49/48, equating 7/6 and 8/7 - fancy math speak for saying you get an interval smack dab in the middle of both 8/7 and 7/6..

As the generator flattens out of mavila range, it stops feeling like a fifth and becomes something else entirely.

temperaments.name: Casablanca
temperaments.description:
Starling family. Generator is a sharp 11/8 (~545¢). Two generators = 6/5.

We're gettin reeaaal flat now, approaching the 'you call this music?' territory. Two of these sharp tritone-ish generators land you on a minor third, which is kind of a weird way to make a minor third if you ask me.

Check out the 11edo antidiatonic here; uses slightly-off 11th harmonic as a generator, which gives you a spot on 9/7 and 14/9. Pretty crazy harmonies available, though the melodic contour begins to get kind of extreme. Could operate as an excellent framework for 11edo harmony.

temperaments.name: Sixix
temperaments.description:
Sharp 6/5 generator. 3rd and 5th harmonics reached by going down, inverting typical chord construction.

Sixix is to kleismic what mavila is to meantone; a bizarro world where theory flips on its head. With enough stacked generators, gives you scales where both a sharp superpyth-like fifth and a flat mavila-like fifth can coexist in the same mode.

temperaments.name: Amity
temperaments.description:
Five generators = 8/3. Generator is a flat neutral third (~339¢). Works well in 39edo. Basically the dicot version of antidiatonic/mavila.

If you really like the 28/23 neutral third this would be your jam (probably not). In exchange for this AMAZING interval, there's a tradeoff: you need a LOT of generators before anything useful shows up. What a deal.

temperaments.name: Mohajira
temperaments.description:
Neutral thirds temperament. Dicot tuning, e.g. this divides the fifth into 2 parts.

Think of this as the "flat" portion of neutral third temperaments, which when stacked, gives you meantone (the flat fifth temperament). Contains the just 11/9 neutral third, which is the lowest complexity neutral interval, which gives it extra sauce.

temperaments.name: Hemififths
temperaments.description:
Dicot; Two generators = 3/2. Excellent no-fives temperament. Neutral chords out the whazoo.

This is the "accurate" neutral third temperament, where stacking a third gives you a pythagorean fifth. Imagine the diatonic scale with pure fifths, and then just clone it and offset the clone by ~350c. 24edo's 11 limit chords sound fricken NUTS here.

temperaments.name: Suhajira
temperaments.description:
Rastmic clan. Dicot tuning, e.g. this divides the fifth into 2 parts.

This is the "sharp" neutral third temperament, which when stacked, gives you superpyth fifths. Evil twin of mohajira.

temperaments.name: Sephiroth
temperaments.description:
A no-3s and no-7s restriction of magic. Generator is a sharp neutral third between 360¢ and 377¢ - so sharp that your fifth extends past 5edo into oneirotonic territory.
Think of it as simultaneously an extremely sharp version of dicot, as well as the antidiatonic equivalent of magic. That is to say;
2 generators gives you an ultra sharp "oneirotonic 3/2", and 5 generators will stack up to a super flat "antidiatonic 3/2". The 10-note MOS is the sweet spot.

temperaments.name: Magic
temperaments.description:
Five major thirds = a twelfth (3/1). Best 9-odd-limit in this complexity range.

In magic, the augmented triad is king - it's the simplest triad in the system, and appears everywhere. You can also play with comma-pumps, as most people are used to 4 stacks of major thirds to cycle back around to an octave in 12edo - here every time you go 'up' an augmented 7th chord, you end up flat of an octave by a quarter tone. Pretty accurate 5/4, but fifths are expensive to reach, so don't expect familiar scale shapes.

temperaments.name: Myna
temperaments.description:
Minor third generator. Named after starling family (126/125).

The name is a double pun: myna birds belong to the starling family of birds, and "myna" sounds like "minor" with a jersey accent. Scales here start to collapse melodically into 4edo cluster temperaments; really difficult to find useable stuff here.

temperaments.name: Superkleismic
temperaments.description:
Sharp minor third. Three generators = 7/4.

Kleismic's sharper, 7-limit cousin. Since only 3 generators give you 7/4, this is a go-to temperament if you want xen sounds + 7 limit harmony. 41edo is a go-to tuning here. Also check out the 26edo 4L 3s scale here; a bizarre minor-ish scale with completely pure 7/4 and 8/7s.

temperaments.name: Orgone
temperaments.description:
2.7.11 subgroup. Generator is ~77/64. Two generators = 16/11, three = 7/4.

The sharper twin of superkleismic, where 3 generators gives you a slightly sharp 7/4. You also have access to that terrible 16/11 interval without having to make an unlistenable temperament in the 650c region. 37edo is especially powerful here, with the just 16/11 | 11/8, and the very accurate, 4c sharp 7/4.

temperaments.name: Rarity
temperaments.description:
2.3.5.19.23 subgroup. Made out of stacking the 23/19 vicesimotertial supraminor third. Yea try saying that out loud.

It doesn't really do too much else though; rarity is an especially unique temperament in that theres nothing good here at all. In a world of crazy temperaments, just intervals and cluster chords, Rarity is a complete standout in that it just... fails to do what everything else does.

temperaments.name: Aurora
temperaments.description: Keegic family. No-threes subgroup. Generator is a near-9/7 or sharp sub-fourth (~450¢). Tempers out the diesis (128/125). Logarithmic phi is in this interval region, which is fun.

temperaments.name: Coditone
temperaments.description:
Ditonmic family. Generator sits right on the Pythagorean ditone, 81/64 (~407.8¢) - the "wrong" major third you get from stacking four pure fifths and refusing to temper anything.

Considering this whole tempering business came about as a way to try and avoid the 81/64 interval and get 5/4 instead, theres some intense irony that comes from defining a temperament around stacking it. Not only is this a stupid idea harmonically, it melodically clusters around 3edo as well. Mathematically optimized for being terrible.

temperaments.name: Roman
temperaments.description:
2.3.5.7 subgroup, also known as "crusher" in its 7-limit form. Generator is ~63/50 (POTE ~414.55¢); seven of them stack to 4/3.

Canonical tunings are 23, 26 and 29edo.

temperaments.name: Sqrtphi
temperaments.description:
Generated by the square root of the golden ratio (~416.55¢), so two generators stack to acoustic phi (833.09¢)

Unlike most temperaments this isn't really a JI approximation at all; the generator is irrational by construction, so it tempers out nothing exactly and instead lands as far from every low-complexity ratio as it can. That's the whole point.

Now, while we SAY that, it is just a bit flat of 14/11, so you get some peculiar 7.11 limit harmony which isn't too bad. But yea, we basically tuned this to be... not in tune.

temperaments.name: Bossier
temperaments.description:
Generator is a sharp 14/11 (CWE ~421.24¢), and eight of them give you 7/1.

Sits directly above sqrtphi and inherits the 14/11 boundary from it.

temperaments.name: Squares
temperaments.description:
Four generators stack to = 8/3. Generator is a sharp supermajor third (~426¢).

Also known as "skwares." if you wanted to be quirky and random xd

The generator sits between 14/11 and 9/7, giving a sort of supermajor augmented feel, but also handing you fifths and fourths if you stack high enough.

temperaments.name: Hamity
temperaments.description:
Amity family. Generator is a near-9/7 (~429–432¢). Five generators reach 3/2. Generator is half of the amity generator + an octave.

The "h" in hamity stands for "half-," though it ends up just sounding like a reference to deli meats than it does to anything musical.

temperaments.name: Novisept
temperaments.description:
2.9.7.11.17 subgroup. Generator is ~434¢ (9/7), stacked 5 times until it becomes 7/4. 11 and 25edo are canonical tunings.

Dont't tell anyone, but I made this one up. I know, I know, but we had a gap in a temperament range here and it has a nice sound. Called Novisept because we're stacking an interval with both 9 and 7 in it, until it becomes just 7.

temperaments.name: Baldi
temperaments.description:
2.9.5.7.13 subgroup. Derived from every other generator of garibaldi. Generator ~200–207¢.

You can also just think of this as every other generator from pythagorean - so its a wholetone scale temperament. Just a biiig stack of wholetones, but with a weird comma-pump thing goin instead of wrapping back around like 6edo does.

temperaments.name: Machine
temperaments.description:
2.7 subgroup. Generator is a flat 8/7.

Imagine if we took the wholetone-like temperament of baldi but tuned it a bit better; Now you have both 4/3 and 3/2 after 8 and 9 generators, and the melodic spacing between the steps feels less stupid!

temperaments.name: Kumonga
temperaments.description:
Starling family. Generator is a sharp 8/7. Tempers out 126/125. You can think of Kumonga as an antidiatonic/mavila tricot; 3 generators gives you an extremely flat mavila fifth.

You cannot imagine how many strings I had to pull to find out what temperament could go here, the amount of research I had to do - and the result? Kumonga. Ok.

Maybe you can make something work here. Prove these lousy tuning theorists wrong. I believe in you.

temperaments.name: Laconic
temperaments.description:
Three 10/9 whole tones stack up to a 3/2.

Generator is an extremely sharp 10/9 (~225¢ in 16edo, ~229¢ in 21edo) - sharp enough that three of them reach a very flat fifth, giving antidiatonic behavior where major and minor invert. Basically, its tricot but we're seriously fudging the numbers. 37edo, 16edo and 21edo are the go-to tunings.

temperaments.name: Tricot / Slendric
temperaments.description:
Three 8/7 generators = 3/2. 2.3.7 subgroup. Very accurate.

Historically this temperament has been called slendric, because in the Indonesian Gamelan scale Slendro, some might say their fifth is ~roughly~ divided into 3 steps - even though the step sizes aren't evenly spaced at all.

So it would be way easier to just call this temperament tricot, meaning we divided the fifth into 3.

temperaments.name: Hemipyth
temperaments.description: Half-octave period. Irrational subgroup based on square roots of Pythagorean intervals. Generator is √(3/2) ≈ 351¢ mapped as ~248¢ within the 600¢ period. Two generators = 3/2.

temperaments.name: Doublewide
temperaments.description: Half-octave period. 2.3.5.7 subgroup. Generator is a sharp ~6/5, four of which plus a 600¢ period give the 3rd harmonic. Equates 25/24, 49/48, and 36/35.. 48edo is an excellent tuning.

temperaments.name: Glacier / Pentacot
temperaments.description:
Pentacot tuning (divides 3/2 into 5 steps). Generator ~137–144¢.

Honestly, do me a favor and just call this pentacot.

temperaments.name: Bohpier
temperaments.description:
Related to Bohlen-Pierce with octave period. 13 generators = 3rd harmonic, 19 = 5th, 23 = 7th.

Basically someone took the bohlen pierce scale, where you divide 3/1 into 13 even steps, and fudged it up so that it fits into an octave. Fun stuff.

temperaments.name: Pluto
temperaments.description:
Pluto's back, and with a vengeance. Similar to its dwarf-planet namesake, nobody really cares about it.

7 bright generator stacks give you a fifth. Generator is a flat 7/5 tritone (~585¢).

This temperament is notable because its built on a near-just 10/7; otherwise, it is just terrible to compose in. All of your melodic steps end up being like 30c apart. Hats off to you if you make this one work.

temperaments.name: Tritonic
temperaments.description:
Marvel family. Generator is a 10/7 tritone (~617.5¢). 5 generators = 6th harmonic. Pretty much at the absolute limit of listenable music.

'Oops! All tritones!'

temperaments.name: Alphatricot
temperaments.description:
Divides 3/1 into 3 equal approximations of 13/9 (~636.6c). Generator ~628.5–640¢.

This temperament used to just be called tricot. However it behaved completely differently from all over n-cot tunings, and instead of dividing 3/2 into 3, it divided 3/1 into 3.
Which is dumb and I hate it.
So after endless complaining and petitioning on forums and wiki spaces, Tricot was renamed to Alphatricot (Alpha n-cot divides 3/1 into n), and Slendric is now correctly being named tricot.

temperaments.name: A-team
temperaments.description:
2.3.5.7 subgroup. Generator between 5\13 and 11\28, defined as ' every other step of tricot/slendric'. Since tricot is 3 steps to a fifth, using every 2 steps of that generator will lead you to avoiding fifths entirely.

Using a generator in this range uniquely avoids having a 3/2 ratio in any reasonably sized scale, which lends to challenging but extremely interesting sounds and structures to compose in. Prototypical oneirotonic (5L 3s) temperament. Works well for gamelan-like scales.

temperaments.name: Buzzard
temperaments.description:
Alpha tetracot (splits 3/1 into 4 steps). Given 3/1 is split into 4 steps, if you put more than 4 steps in your scale you'll get a fifth! Funny how that works out.

Generator ~471.4–480¢. Prototypical hard oneirotonic(5L 3s) tuning. Creates 5edo cluster temperament scales, since the generator is so close to 5edo's 3/2. As a secondary consequence, only large edos tend to hit this range; 53edo, 43edo, and 33edo fit here. Works well for gamelan scales.

temperaments.name: Kleismic
temperaments.description:
Alpha hexacot (splits 3/1 into 6 steps). Generator ~314.3–320¢.

Head of one of the largest temperament families in xenharmonic theory. Six 6/5 minor thirds stack to a perfect twelfth. All of the 4L 3s scales here feel like xen variations of minor scales; lots of phrygian and double harmonic minor sounds that result from the substantially large step size.

temperaments.name: Nusecond
temperaments.description: Starling family. Generator is ~49/45 neutral second. Two generators = 6/5. It&#39s made up of neutral seconds, if you could believe it.

temperaments.name: Hemikleismic
temperaments.description: Kleismic family. Splits 6/5 in half, generating a neutral second of 35/32. Two neutral seconds = one minor third. The resulting melodic landscape of ~155¢ steps doesn't map to anything in 12edo.

temperaments.name: Porcupine
temperaments.description: Two generators = 6/5, three = 4/3. ~163¢ generator.

temperaments.name: Superpine
temperaments.description:
Like porcupine but has flat fifths. Generator is 1/3 of a fourth (~35/32). Needs 15-tone MOS (7L 8s) for harmonics beyond 3.

You can think of this as basically being the anti-diatonic version of Tetracot; 4 stacks give you an extremely flat mavila fifth.

temperaments.name: Ammonite
temperaments.description:
Porcupine family. Generator is a sharp fifth (~747¢). Eight generators reach 5/4. 13-note MOS is the sweet spot.

Named after the extinct cephalopod, continuing the animal-themed naming convention of the porcupine family.

I kind of understood why "hedgehog" would be related to porcupine, but they lose me here.

temperaments.name: Sensamagic
temperaments.description: Tempers out 245/243. Two generators of ~440¢ approximate 6/5 + 9/7. Divides 3/2 into 7/6 and 10/9.

temperaments.name: Sensi
temperaments.description:
Half a major sixth generator. Two generators = 5/3, seven = 6/1.

Originally called "semisixths" (semi-major-sixth), later shortened to "sensi" in a naming convention cleanup. Where'd the "m" go??

temperaments.name: Würschmidt
temperaments.description:
Sharp major third generator. Eight generators = 6/1. Named after José Würschmidt. Who? Why? Good question.

The opposite approach of meantone; whereas meantone reaches 5/4 through stacking 3/2, Würschmidt reaches 3/2 the hard way through stacking a very accurate 5/4. 31 and 34edo are best bets for having both a decent 3/2 and 5/4, but if you don't care about 3/2 accuracy then 28edo is just a diabolical stack of purely accurate 5/4 thirds.

Also creates 3edo cluster scales which are exceptionally hard to write in melodically. But by god, those augmented chords almost make the price worth it. Almost.

temperaments.name: Magus
temperaments.description:
Sharper analogue of Würschmidt in the sensamagic clan. Generator is a sharp ~5/4. Three generators reach 128/125 short of the octave; eleven generators reach 3/2.

Idk I just wanted something sharper of "Würschmidt" to fill out more space frankly.

temperaments.name: Neominor
temperaments.description:
Breedsmic temperament. Generator is a subminor third. 4L 5s, 4L 9s, 4L 13s MOS family.

Breedsmic. Seriously who comes up with these names?

You'll notice that this is the last temperament as we approach ~300c; this is because its the last catalogued and frankly usable rank 2 temperament as we approach the bounds of 4edo (300c). As we get closer to 300c, all MOS scales start to collapse into 4edo cluster temperaments, where have basically 4edo + a bunch of tiny comma steps.

temperaments.name: Orwell
temperaments.description:
Subminor third (7/6) generator. Seven generators = twelfth. Excellent 11-limit.

Named because the generator is 19 steps of 84edo, splitting "1984" into "19" and "84." A literary pun turned tuning system. I hate it.

temperaments.name: Lovecraft
temperaments.description:
No-threes subgroup (2.5.7.13). If it wasn't obvious, no-threes just means it sucks at approximating 3/2, but decently approximates intervals that involve other prime numbers. Generator is a subminor third between Orwell and Neominor territory (~277¢).

Continuing the trend of naming temperaments after authors with tenuous connection. Thankfully not named after his cat.

temperaments.name: Semaphore
temperaments.description:
Semi-fourth: two generators = 4/3. Equates 7/6 and 8/7.

The name is a pun on "semi-fourth." If the tuning equates both 9/8 and 10/9 (which it does in 19 and 43 edo), it produces godzilla temperament.

Why is it named godzilla? Good question.

temperaments.name: Tetracot
temperaments.description:
Four generators = 3/2. Generator is a sub-major second (~176¢). EDOs: 27, 34, 41.

The OG n-cot tuning. The name sounded so cool that we renamed a bunch of other temperaments in its wake. Sort of. To varying degrees of success.

temperaments.name: Didacus
temperaments.description:
Tempers out 3136/3125. Generator is half a major third (half of 5/4).

Two generators = 5/4, five generators = 7/4. Similar to baldi in that it can approximate that wholetone scale "dreamy" feel, but with a flat generator instead of sharp. You can also try thinking of this as the super sharp version of tetracot, where four generators give you an extremely sharp superfifth.

temperaments.name: Emka
temperaments.description:
Hemimean clan. Generator is near 11/8. 11 and 13 note MOS scales. Basically the canonical 37edo temperament made by stacking its hyper-accurate 11/8.

Can make some pretty gnarly 11 and 13 limit sounds. 9 stacks gives you an accurate 5/4. Check out the 2L 7s scale if you want to scrunch some faces.

temperaments.name: Thuja
temperaments.description:
Buzzardsmic clan. Generator is ~11/8 (~558.6¢). Twelve generators reach 3/1.

I actually love this name. Rolls off the tongue. Well, there's no tongue involved. Spits out of the mouth? Anyways, say it with me; Thuja. Thoo-jaaa. Yea.

temperaments.name: Octacot
temperaments.description:
Tetracot family. Eight generators = 3/2. Half of a tetracot generator.

Continuing the trend of tetracot; dividing tetra into 2 = octa. Eight steps of 88¢ = 704¢, just 2 cents sharp of a pure 3/2.

temperaments.name: Passion
temperaments.description: Near-12edo generator (~98¢). Twelve generators = octave minus a comma.... Basically 12edo with one warped large step, resulting in a scale that has really bad fifths.

temperaments.name: Heptacot
temperaments.description:
Splits the perfect fifth into seven ~100¢ semitones.

Effectively a 12edo cluster temperament; either you have 12edo, or very large EDOs who form a mos that clusters around 12 large steps and very tiny small steps. You basically can use this as a simple framework to "Detemper" 12edo into something that isn't just intonation, such as a much larger EDO.

temperaments.name: Escape
temperaments.description: Escapade family. Twenty-one generators = octave. Very small generator ~56¢. You can probably get some cool somewhat-detempered 21edo structures out of this. Honestly that's the only reason I can see one wanting to use temperaments like this; warping an EDO and then composing in a scale within that warped edo. You'll find thats the case for most every temperament that forms out of stacking a small interval.

temperaments.name: Valentine
temperaments.description:
Generator is ~77.1¢. Fifteen generators = 3/2. Excellent 11-limit accuracy.

Probably too many generators to reach a fifth if you ask me but what can ya say. Basically describes 15L 1s (and is thus bounded by 16 and 15edo).

temperaments.name: Diaschismic
temperaments.description:
Diaschismic. Half-octave period. More accurate cousin of pajara. Gen ~104¢.

The diaschisma (2048/2025) was known to classical tuning theorists long before anyone thought to build a temperament around it.

temperaments.name: Pajara
temperaments.description:
Half-octave period (~600¢). Decatonic scales. 22edo optimal. Gen ~108¢.

Sounds good, 10/10 would recommend

temperaments.name: Injera
temperaments.description:
Half-octave period. Meantone family; tempers out 81/80 and 50/49. 12edo is the simplest tuning; 26edo is more characteristic. Gen ~94¢.

Essentially two parallel meantone chains a tritone apart. 38edo (= two parallel 19edos) also works. however, it melodically is pretty weak - a whole bunch of ~90c half steps and tritones everywhere.

temperaments.name: Blackwood
temperaments.description:
1/5-octave period. Tempers out 256/243. Think of it as two offsets of 5edo. 15edo, 20, 25edo are core tunings.

Named after Easley Blackwood Jr. (1933–2023), who composed the landmark Twelve Microtonal Etudes in 1980. Absolute legend. Every note in a blackwood scale can root a major or minor triad, which is a wild property for a non-12 system.

temperaments.name: Whitewood
temperaments.description:
1/7-octave period. 21, 28, and 35edo are core tunings. Dual of blackwood - divides the octave into 7 equal parts instead of 5.

The mirror image of blackwood: Here we use the flat 7edo fifth vs the sharp 5edo fifth. Like Blackwood, has alternating major and minor chords on every note. All diatonic modes work in all keys simultaneously.

temperaments.name: Augmented
temperaments.description:
1/3-octave period. Three 5/4 = octave. Major third generator ~400¢.

You've heard this one without knowing it. Any time an augmented triad sounds like it "closes" in 12edo, you're hearing augmented temperament at work; the tempering of 3 major thirds to be an octave. The augmented triad IS the tonic chord of this system. Lives in all EDOs divisible by 3.

It also sounds bad lmao

temperaments.name: August
temperaments.description: 1/3-octave period. Extends augmented with 7-limit by tempering out 225/224. Generator is a sharpened chromatic semitone. 15edo is the simplest tuning.

temperaments.name: Triforce
temperaments.description:
1/3-octave period. Divides the period into logarithmic-phi-sized fractions. Generator is ~35/32 (~153¢). Equates 7/6 and 8/7 via 49/48. 24edo and 39edo are good tunings.

For an augmented / 1\3 period tuning, its pretty good. You got fifths, major chords, augmented chords, etc.

Yes, it's named after that Triforce.

temperaments.name: Diminished
temperaments.description:
1/4-octave period. Four 6/5 = octave. Minor third generator ~300¢.

This is one temperament most classically-trained musicians already know. The octatonic scale (alternating whole and half steps) IS the diminished temperament's MOS in 12edo. The diminished seventh chord as four equally-spaced minor thirds is literally just 4edo. You've been using it all along.

temperaments.name: Lemba
temperaments.description:
Half-octave period. Generator ~230¢ near golden ratio of half-octave.

One generator plus one period comes remarkably close to phi (~1.618), which means the Fibonacci-ratio harmonics 8:13:21:34:55 are all well-approximated. Lemba simultaneously approximates acoustic phi AND logarithmic phi, a rare mathematical coincidence that makes number theorists unreasonably happy. Does that mean it sounds good? Of course not.

temperaments.name: Hedgehog
temperaments.description: Half-octave period. Porcupine-family. 22edo is the canonical tuning.

temperaments.name: Astrology
temperaments.description:
Half-octave period. Five ~5/4 generators give the 3rd harmonic. Related to magic family. 22edo and 16edo are core tunings.

If anyone ever starts talking to you about "astrology temperament," they're either a tuning theorist or deeply confused about their horoscope. Either way steer clear of them.

temperaments.name: Miracle
temperaments.description:
The secor (~116.7¢). Six generators = a fifth. Exceptional 11-limit efficiency.

Stands for "Multiple Integer Ratios Approximated Consistently, Linearly and Evenly." Which is uh, what most all temperaments seek out to do? Has historical importance as one of the first xen temperaments really defined in the 1970s.

temperaments.name: Negri
temperaments.description:
Large semitone generator. Four generators = 4/3.

Named after John Negri, who published a "10-out-of-19 maximally even scale" in the journal Interval back in 1986. Previously called "quadrafourths."

Wait, why did we change the name from quadrafourths???

temperaments.name: Unknown Diatonic
temperaments.description: Diatonic range from 7n to 5n but for 2x octave periods. Good 3.5.7 approximations within the period. I think it sounds cool and probably should be better defined idk
